claims.text: Cantor-type high-entropy alloys can exhibit high corrosion resistance.
The proposed coarse-grained Cantor-type baseline has an intact, protective native oxide film.
Sliding contact in chloride solution induces severe plastic deformation in the HEA surface.
Sliding-induced deformation dynamically refines the HEA surface grains to the ultra-nanocrystalline regime.
Sliding-induced deformation partially amorphizes the HEA surface.
Ultra-nanocrystalline grain refinement can soften an HEA surface through inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Refinement and amorphization lower surface shear strength, thereby lowering friction and wear.
Sliding mechanically disrupts the protective passive oxide film.
The increased grain-boundary density produced by refinement impairs repassivation.
Reduced passive-film stability increases corrosion damage.
Stress introduction and grain refinement can reduce the corrosion resistance of a Cantor alloy.
Passive-film disruption under sliding accelerates localized corrosion.
The coupled tribo-corrosion response is governed by competition between reduced mechanical wear and increased corrosion damage.
The tribo-corrosion specimen will have a lower wear rate than the inert-sliding baseline because of its refined, lubricious surface.
The tribo-corrosion specimen will have a higher corrosion rate than the static chloride-immersion baseline.
Accelerated corrosion can offset the predicted reduction in wear, making total tribo-corrosion degradation similar to or greater than degradation under isolated conditions.
During static chloride immersion, the passive film remains largely undisturbed.
The prediction should apply only to passivating HEAs that undergo dynamic amorphization during sliding.
Rapid self-healing of the passive film can cause the proposed prediction to fail.
The hypothesis requires total tribo-corrosion degradation to exceed the sum of isolated wear and corrosion effects.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows total degradation to be merely similar to or greater than degradation in either isolated condition, whereas the falsification rule requires total degradation to exceed the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion effects. The latter is a substantially stronger superadditivity requirement and could reject outcomes that the prediction explicitly permits.
